Two generation modes defined by the benchmark: Cascade (checklist, then skeleton, then code) and E2E (code directly). Agent scaffolding and model snapshots not stated

fields.v: GPT-5 best overall (avg 29.6; Level 3 44.6), Gemini 2.5-flash 15.5, GPT-3.5-turbo 2.7; open-source models low; coding models 0.0-7.5 at Level 3. E2E beats Cascade at Level 1 for Gemini-2.5-flash (16.7 vs 7.3) and GPT-5 (23.1 vs 12.6), and by at least 2.5 points for GPT-oss-20B, Llama-3.3-70B and Phi-4-14B; at Level 2 the E2E advantage persists only for Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen-3-30B favours Cascade (GPT-5 Cascade 34.6 vs E2E 33.2). Language: JavaScript highest overall average (9.0 vs Python 7.6, Java 5.7); authors say Python remains dominant among closed-source models, but Table 5 averages give Python highest only for GPT-5 (32.7 vs JS 32.5) and GPT-3.5-turbo (3.2 vs 2.7), while Gemini-2.5-flash is highest in JavaScript (17.0 vs Python 15.5). ALE improves all five models (+3.2 to +38.7 points). No significance tests

fields.v: Distinguished models (wide spread between closed- and open-source), modes and languages. Not repeated (single Pass@1 run at temperature 0). Limitations stated: some models cannot use temperature 0 and outputs vary across hardware; cascaded test points amplify small deviations (observed once in ALE); undetectable agent 'cheating' (hard-coded outputs, mocked responses); occasional timeouts from OS, VM, browser or network; CodeBLEU indicators less accurate than Pass@1

fields.v: Limitations: agent 'cheating' not detectable; environment timeouts (internet needed for packages, VM slowdowns, I/O, slow page loads); LLM instability despite temperature 0. Authors' conclusions: E2E mitigates the 'Chinese Whispers' degradation of hierarchical document handovers; language preference context-dependent. Gaps / future work: multimodal benchmark (UI vision, console output, spoken prompts); whether instability can be mitigated is an open question

fields.v: Inconsistencies: in Table 3 the Avg. row gives 4.8 in the Avg. column, below every per-setting average (4.4-8.1); the mean of the 11 per-model averages is about 7.6 (p. 12); text says the Level 2 E2E advantage 'persisted only for Llama-3.3-70B', but rebuilt Table 3 also gives Phi4-14B E2E L2 6.2 vs Cascade L2 3.1 (p. 11-12); text says Python 'remains dominant among closed-source agents', but Table 5 gives Gemini-2.5-flash JS 17.0 > Python 15.5 (p. 14); ALE gains in text and Table 6 do not all match the before/after values: GPT-5-mini Python→JavaScript 63.2→93.3 is +30.1 but reported +31.1; Gemini Python→Java +16.7 (values give 16.8), Gemma3-27B +3.2 (3.3) and +6.0 (6.1), rounding (p. 14-15); PV similarity metric defined as 'strings cosine similarity' in the text but as Levenshtein distance in Table 2 and the Table 4 caption (p. 10, 13); test points described as cascading ('if the former one fails, the following will never get passed', p. 11; deviations cause complete project failures, p. 17) yet §7.2 says isolated timeout errors 'will not propagate to subsequent test points' (p. 17); Table 6 caption repeats 'Bold emphasizes the difference between ProjectEvalPlus and its peers' (p. 15); 'theoretically proves' support for all languages without a formal proof (p. 9). Table 1, Table 4 and Table 5 open-source rows are jumbled in the extracted text and not used; the Table 3 open-source rows were rebuilt by reading the numbers row by row (6 per model), checked against each row's Avg and the column Avg row; the Table 5 closed-source rows (18 values each) read cleanly. 'LLM agents' are models; no agent framework named. Repository: https://github.com/RyanLoil/ProjectEvalPlus/ (open source). Pre-registration: not claimed. Programming languages: Python, Java, JavaScript (testcodes in Python)
